rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After praising the Qur’an as wisdom, guidance, and mercy, the passage condemns those who trade it for amusement and thereby mislead others.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر من صفات القرآن الحكمة، وأنه هدى ورحمة، وأن متبعه فائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is said to have been revealed about al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who bought Persian books and told Quraysh tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar.
rows.anchor: ونزلت هذه الآية في النضر بن الحارث، كان يتجر إلى فارس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another occasion report identifies Ibn Khatal, who bought a singing slave woman who insulted people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في ابن خطل، اشترى جارية تغني بالسب

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة عن النبي
rows.claim: A report from Abu Umama says the Prophet declared buying and selling singing women forbidden and recited this verse.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث من رواية أبي أمامة، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak explains “idle talk” as associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: لهو الحديث: الشرك

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن جريج
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj explain “idle talk” as the drum, a kind of musical instrument.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وابن جريج: الطبل، وهذا ضرب من آلة الغناء

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata interprets “idle talk” as trivialities.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: الترهات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported meanings include magic and the insults exchanged by people of pre-Islamic times.
rows.anchor: وقيل: السحر. وقيل: ما كان يشتغل به أهل الجاهلية من السباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An additional interpretation is anything that distracts a person from worshipping God; jokes, fables, and singing are also listed.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا: ما شغلك عن عبادة الله، وذكره من السحر

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl identifies idle talk with religious disputation and immersion in falsehood.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل: الجدال في الدين والخوض في الباطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Buying” is metaphorical for choosing something and devoting one’s reason to it; it is literal for a purchased singer or book.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الشراء هنا مجاز عن اختيار الشيء، وصرف عقله بكليته إليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows the annexation to mean a portion of speech that is itself amusement.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن تكون الإضافة بمعنى من التبعيضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The annexation “idle talk” means talk that is objectionable or condemned.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالحديث: الحديث المنكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read the verb with an open yāʾ; the other seven canonical readers use a ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير، وأبو عمرو: ليضل بفتح الياء، وباقي السبعة: بضمها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: With the open-yāʾ reading, the act may mean persisting in one’s existing error and increasing in it.
rows.anchor: قلت: معنيان، أحدهما: ليثبت على ضلاله الذي كان عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Alternatively, “to mislead” may stand for “to be misled,” since a person who misleads must already be astray.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن يوضع ليضل موضع ليضل من قبل أن من أضل كان ضالا لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Without knowledge” means buying without commercial understanding or discernment, exchanging error for guidance and falsehood for truth.
rows.anchor: قلت: لما جعله مشتريا لهو الحديث بالقرآن قال: يشتري بغير علم بالتجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God’s path” is explained in two ways: Islam or the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وسبيل الله: الإسلام أو القرآن، قولان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers that the verse concern amusement joined to unbelief, explaining its severe language about misleading from God’s path.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والذي يترجح إن الآية نزلت في لهو الحديث مضافا إلى الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Hafs read “and takes it” in the accusative, coordinated with “to mislead”; the remaining readers use the nominative, coordinated with “buys.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة، والكسائي، وحفص: ويتخذها، بالنصب عطفا على ليضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “and takes it” most naturally refers to God’s path; other proposals refer it to the Qur’anic signs or to reports generally.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عود ضمير ويتخذها على السبيل، كقوله: ويبغونها عوجا

rows.speaker: صاحب التحرير
rows.claim: The author of al-Taḥrīr proposes that “idle talk” means reports used to bolster opponents’ religion and deter followers from faith; rulers paid bribes for this advocacy.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب التحرير: ويظهر لي أنه أراد بلهو الحديث: ما كانوا يظهرونه من الأحاديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun in “who buys” is singular and begins a sequence that shifts between singular and plural agreement.
rows.anchor: ومن في: من يشتري موصولة، ونظيره في من الشرطية قوله: ومن يؤمن بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an has two instances of agreement shifting from a relative’s singular wording to plural meaning and back to singular wording.
rows.anchor: ولا نعلم جاء في القرآن ما حمل على اللفظ، ثم على المعنى، ثم على اللفظ، غير هاتين الآيتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse condemns the buyer through successive traits: turning from wisdom, arrogance, ignoring its recitation, and acting as though deaf to it.
rows.anchor: وتضمنت هذه الآية ذم المشتري من وجوه التولية عن الحكمة، ثم الاستكبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “As though he had not heard it” is circumstantial to the arrogant person; the following comparison may be a further circumstance.
rows.anchor: وكأن لم يسمعها: حال من الضمير في مستكبرا، أي مشبها حال من لم يسمعها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows the two simile clauses to stand as independent sentences.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يكونا استئنافين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning painful punishment for unbelievers, the passage turns to the promise made to believers.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر ما وعد به الكفار من العذاب الأليم، ذكر ما وعد به المؤمنين

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads “abiding” with a wāw; the majority read it with a yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: خالدون، بالواو والجمهور: بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God’s promise” reinforces the promise itself, while “truly” reinforces the distinct assertion about gardens.
rows.anchor: وانتصب وعد الله على أنه مصدر مؤكد لنفسه، وحقا على المصدر المؤكد لغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Noble” praises created kinds either for precious beauty or for the excellence and ordered craft of every kind.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كريم: مدحته بكرم جوهره ونفاسته وحسن منظره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This is God’s creation” points to the created things listed and challenges the unbelievers with the evidence they display.
rows.anchor: هذا خلق الله إشارة إلى ما ذكر من مخلوقاته، وبخ بذلك الكفار وأظهر حجته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “creation” means the created object, as in the expression “a dirham minted by the prince.”
rows.anchor: والخلق بمعنى المخلوق، كقولهم: درهم ضرب الأمير، أي مضروبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge asks what the idols created after God’s creatures have been listed; “what” can be a relative object or an interrogative joined to a relative.
rows.anchor: ويجوز في ماذا أن تكون كلها موصولة بمعنى الذي، وتكون مفعولا ثانيا لأروني

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh records the uncommon use of the whole expression “mādhā” as a single relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: واستعمال ماذا كلها موصولا قليل، وقد ذكره سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from reproaching the idolaters to judging them manifestly confused, since they abandon their creator for an idol.
rows.anchor: ثم أضرب عن توبيخهم وتبكيتهم إلى التسجيل عليهم بأنهم في حيرة واضحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports disagree over whether Luqman was free or enslaved; if free, some identify him as Ibn Baʿura.
rows.anchor: اختلف في لقمان، أكان حرا أم عبدا؟ فإذا قلنا: كان حرا، فقيل: هو ابن باعورا

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says Luqman was Job’s sister’s son; Muqatil instead calls him Job’s maternal cousin.
rows.anchor: قال وهب: ابن أخت أيوب عليه السلام. وقال مقاتل: ابن خالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report makes Luqman a descendant of Azar, living a thousand years and learning from David; he stopped issuing rulings when David became a prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان من أولاد آزر، وعاش ألف سنة، وأدرك داود عليه السلام، وأخذ منه العلم

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: In the report, Luqman explains that he stopped giving rulings by asking, “Should I not be content when you have been provided for?”
rows.anchor: فقيل له: لم؟ فقال: ألا أكتفي إذا كفيت؟

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi calls Luqman a judge among the Children of Israel and places him between Jesus and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقال الواقدي: كان قاضيا في بني إسرائيل، وزمانه ما بين عيسى ومحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most authorities deny that Luqman was a prophet; Ikrima and al-Shaʿbi say that he was.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على أنه لم يكن نبيا. وقال عكرمة، والشعبي: كان نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report about Luqman’s enslaved identity and ethnicity begins by naming Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Mujahid as authorities.
rows.anchor: وإذا قلنا: كان عبدا، اختلف في جنسه، فقال ابن عباس، وابن المسيب، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman is described as a Nubian with split feet and thick lips; al-Farraʾ and others instead call him Abyssinian, with a cut nose and thick lip.
rows.anchor: كان نوبيا مشقق الرجلين ذا مشافر. وقال الفراء وغيره: كان حبشيا مجدوع الأنف ذا مشفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports variously make Luqman a carpenter, upholsterer, tailor, shepherd, or servant who gathered firewood daily.
rows.anchor: واختلف فيما كان يعانيه من الأشغال، فقال خالد بن الربيع: كان نجارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects recording these unstable reports about Luqman’s freedom, ethnicity, and occupation; commentators should leave them aside.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاضطراب في كونه حرا أو عبدا، وفي جنسه، وفيما كان يعانيه، يوجب أن لا يكتب شيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: One saying calls the worst person the one who does not care that others see him doing wrong.
rows.anchor: قيل له: أي الناس شر؟ قال: الذي لا يبالي أن يراه الناس مسيئا

rows.speaker: لقمان
rows.claim: Luqman tells David he awoke “in another’s hand,” prompting David to reflect and swoon.
rows.anchor: وقال له داود، عليه السلام، يوما: كيف أصبحت؟ قال: أصبحت في يد غيري

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says he read more than ten thousand examples of Luqman’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه: قرأت في حكم لقمان أكثر من عشرة آلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom here means instructive speech that people retain and transmit because it awakens reflection.
rows.anchor: والحكمة: المنطق الذي يتعظ به ويتنبه به، ويتناقله الناس لذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads “that you give thanks” as explanatory, since granting wisdom entails instruction; true wisdom is acted upon through worship and gratitude.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: أن هي المفسرة، لأن إيتاء الحكمة في معنى القول

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads “that you give thanks” as an infinitival clause expressing purpose: wisdom was granted so Luqman would thank God.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: المعنى: ولقد آتينا لقمان الحكمة لأن يشكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude benefits the grateful person, not God, who is independent of it; disbelief cannot harm Him, and He deserves praise in essence and attributes.
rows.anchor: فإنما يشكر لنفسه: أي ثواب الشكر لا يحصل إلا للشاكرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “When he said” can mean “remember when he said,” or “We gave him wisdom when he said,” with the earlier verb elided.
rows.anchor: وإذ قال: أي واذكر إذ، وقيل: يحتمل أن يكون التقدير: وآتيناه الحكمة، إذ قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase describing Luqman’s son as “barr” is explained as beneficent or thankful.
rows.anchor: وابنه بار، أي: أو أنعم، أو اشكر، أو شاكر، أقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Luqman’s son and wife were unbelievers, but he kept advising them until they accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: قيل: كان ابنه وامرأته كافرين، فما زال يعظهما حتى أسلما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading makes “associating partners is a great injustice” part of Luqman’s speech; a separate divine statement is also proposed.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: إن الشرك لظلم عظيم من كلام لقمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim’s authentic collection contains a report that appears to treat the warning against shirk as Luqman’s own words.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم ما ظاهره أنه من كلام لقمان

rows.speaker: البزي
rows.claim: Al-Bazzi reads “my dear son” with a quiescent yāʾ in the first occurrence, kasra in the middle, and fatḥa in the third.
rows.anchor: وقرأ البزي: يا بني، بالسكون، ويا بني إنها: بكسر الياء، ويا بني أقم: بفتحها

rows.speaker: حفص والمفضل عن عاصم
rows.claim: Hafs and al-Mufaddal from Asim read the yāʾ with fatḥa in all three occurrences, treating it as “yā bunayya” with the alif elided.
rows.anchor: وحفص والمفضل عن عاصم: بالفتح في الثلاثة على تقدير يا بنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining seven canonical readers use kasra in all three forms of “my dear son.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: بالكسر في الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parent command follows Luqman’s warning against shirk as a further call to obey God, then explains why parents deserve kindness.
rows.anchor: ووصينا الإنسان بوالديه: لما بين لقمان لابنه أن الشرك ظلم ونهاه عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the parent command part of Luqman’s advice, which God reports; another makes it God’s words to Luqman.
rows.anchor: فهو من كلام لقمان مما وصى به ابنه، أخبر الله عنه بذلك. وقيل: هو من كلام الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view treats the verse as an insertion reinforcing a child’s obedience to a parent in obeying God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذه الآية اعتراض بين أثناء وصيته للقمان

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi says the correct view is that this verse and 29:8 were revealed concerning Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, as a group of exegetes also held.
rows.anchor: وقال القرطبي: والصحيح أن هذه الآية وآية العنكبوت نزلتا في سعد بن أبي وقاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith gives the mother three shares of filial kindness before the father receives one, because the mother bears pregnancy, birth, nursing, and upbringing.
rows.anchor: في الحديث الأمر ببر الأم ثلاث مرات، ثم ذكر الأب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “weakness upon weakness” as successive hardship and successive stages of creation.
rows.anchor: وهنا على وهن، قال ابن عباس: شدة بعد شدة، وخلقا بعد خلق

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak explains “weakness upon weakness” as weakness repeatedly increasing.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: ضعفا بعد ضعف

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains it as effort upon effort: the weakness of pregnancy, labor, and postpartum recovery.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: جهدا على جهد، يعني: ضعف الحمل، وضعف الطلق، وضعف النفاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first explanations parse the phrase as a circumstantial accusative; an alternative makes it the child’s condition through successive developmental stages.
rows.anchor: وانتصب على هذه الأقوال على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu Amr in one transmission read both occurrences of “wahn” with an open hāʾ; most readers use a quiescent hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى الثقفي، وأبو عمرو في رواية: وهنا على وهن، بفتح الهاء فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open-vowel form may resemble alternate pronunciations of “hair,” or may be the regular accusative verbal noun of “to weaken.”
rows.anchor: فاحتمل أن يكون كالشعر والشعر، واحتمل أن يكون مصدر وهن بكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use “his weaning”; al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Qatada, al-Jahdari, and Yaʿqub read “his separation,” meaning weaning at the end of two years.
rows.anchor: وقرأوا: وفصاله. وقرأ الحسن، وأبو رجاء، وقتادة، والجحدري، ويعقوب: وفصله، ومعناه الفطام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree on two years as the nursing period for rulings and maintenance, but disagree about the period that establishes milk kinship.
rows.anchor: وأجمعوا على اعتبار العامين في مدة الرضاع في باب الأحكام والنفقات

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas prefers reading “that you give thanks to Me” as explanatory rather than infinitival.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس: الأجود أن تكون مفسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thank God for the gift of faith and parents for the gift of upbringing; “to Me is the return” warns during the exhortation.
rows.anchor: لي: أي على نعمة الإيمان. ولوالديك: على نعمة التربية إلي المصير: توعد أثناء الوصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to refuse parents’ demand for shirk was discussed under 29:8; this verse uses “upon” where that verse uses a causal “for.”
rows.anchor: فلا تطعهما: تقدم الكلام عليه في العنكبوت، إلا أن هنا على، وهناك لتشرك بلام العلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In a good manner” describes kind companionship, including feeding and clothing parents, avoiding harshness, visiting illness, and burying them after death.
rows.anchor: وانتصب معروفا على أنه صفة لمصدر محذوف، أي صحابا، أو مصاحبا معروفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the path of those who turn to God means following the Messenger’s path rather than the parents’ path.
rows.anchor: واتبع سبيل من أناب إلي: أي رجع إلى الله، وهو سبيل الرسول لا سبيلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To Me is your return” includes both child and parents, and God will repay each according to deeds.
rows.anchor: أي مرجعك ومرجعهما، فأجازي كلا منكم بعمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After forbidding shirk, Luqman points to God’s power: nothing within His power can escape or be delayed.
rows.anchor: ولما نهى لقمان ابنه عن الشرك، نبهه على قدرة الله، وأنه لا يمكن أن يتأخر عن مقدوره شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it” most naturally refers to the whole matter; Nafi reads “weight” in the nominative, while the other seven make it accusative.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في إنها ضمير القصة. وقرأ نافع: مثقال، بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading makes the verb complete; the masculine “weight” is treated as feminine because it is annexed to a feminine noun.
rows.anchor: على إن تك تامة، وهي قراءة الأعرج وأبي جعفر، وأخبر عن مثقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative reading makes the verb incomplete, with an implied subject; a report says Luqman asked whether God knows a grain at the bottom of the sea.
rows.anchor: وباقي السبعة: بالنصب على إن تك ناقصة

rows.speaker: عبد الكريم الجزري
rows.claim: Abd al-Karim al-Jazari has a reading of “it lies” with a kasra on kāf and a doubled, open nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الكريم الجزري: فتكن، بكسر الكاف وشد النون وفتحها

rows.speaker: محمد بن أبي فجة البعلبكي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Abi Fajja al-Baʿlabakki reads the verb with ḍamma on tāʾ and a doubled open nūn.
rows.anchor: وقراءة محمد بن أبي فجة البعلبكي: فتكن، بضم التاء وفتح الكاف والنون مشددة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reads the verb from “to nest or settle”; the same reading is also transmitted from Abd al-Karim al-Jazari.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة: فتكن، بفتح التاء وكسر الكاف وسكون النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to a concrete thing or to an act of obedience or disobedience; on the accusative reading it may refer to the deed itself.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الضمير ضمير عرض، أي تلك الفعلة من الطاعة أو المعصية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the deed, tiny as a mustard seed and hidden in a rock or anywhere in the universe, will be brought forth for judgment.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فمن نصب يعني مثقال، كان الضمير للهيئة من الإساءة والإحسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is subtle because His knowledge reaches every hidden thing, and expert because He knows its full reality; Qatada adds that He extracts it and knows its location.
rows.anchor: إن الله لطيف، يتوصل علمه إلى كل خفي. خبير: عالم بكنهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The examples move from a hard-to-extract rock to distant heavens and then the familiar earth, building toward the most comprehensive sense.
rows.anchor: وبدأ له بما يتعلق به أولا، وهو كينونة الشيء. في صخرة: وهو ما صلب من الحجر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi identify the rock as the one beneath the earth; Ibn Abbas says it lies under the seven earths and records sinners’ deeds.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس والسدي، أن هذه الصخرة هي التي عليها الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the rock lies beneath the seven earths and records the deeds of wicked people.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي تحت الأرضين السبع، يكتب فيها أعمال الفجار

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reports claims about a rock supporting earth, fish, and water on an angel, or a rock in the wind, but says their chains are weak; the language instead expresses maximal scope.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: قيل: أراد الصخرة التي عليها الأرض والحوت والماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rock, heavens, and earth evoke concealment, distance, and darkness; bringing the grain forth demonstrates God’s knowledge and power.
rows.anchor: ففي صخرة إشارة إلى الحجاب، وفي السموات إشارة إلى البعد، وفي الأرض إشارة إلى الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman orders prayer first as the noblest act of turning toward God, then enjoining good and forbidding wrong, then enduring hardship.
rows.anchor: ولما نهاه أولا عن الشرك، وأخبره ثانيا بعلمه تعالى وباهر قدرته، أمره بما يتوسل به إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience covers all calamities, especially harm caused by enjoining right and forbidding wrong; the adviser should first embody what he teaches.
rows.anchor: ثم بالصبر على ما يصيبه من المحن جميعها، أو على ما يصيبه بسبب الأمر بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” refers to all the preceding commands and prohibitions; “resolute matters” may mean matters resolved upon or matters that are themselves resolute.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك إشارة إلى ما تقدم مما نهاه عنه وأمره به. والعزم مصدر

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj explains these as things God has resolved and commanded.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: مما عزمه الله وأمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers necessary, binding duties because the demonstrative gathers all commands and prohibitions into one reference.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يريد من لازمات الأمور الواجبة، لأن الإشارة بذلك إلى جميع ما أمر به ونهى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman’s advice indicates that these acts were duties across religious communities; “resolve” means controlling and maintaining a matter’s soundness.
rows.anchor: وهذه الطاعات يدل إيصاء لقمان على أنها كانت مأمورا بها في سائر الملل

rows.speaker: مؤرج
rows.claim: Muʾarrij says “ʿazm” means “ḥazm,” firmness or prudence, in the Hudhayli dialect.
rows.anchor: وقال مؤرج: العزم: الحزم، بلغة هذيل

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects al-Mubarrad’s claim that the initial consonant changed between ʿazm and ḥazm, since each word has its own complete derivation.
rows.anchor: وما قاله المبرد من أن العين قلبت حاء ليس بشيء، لا طراد تصاريف كل واحد من اللفظين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والجماعة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and most exegetes explain “do not turn your cheek” as turning away in pride; face people without arrogance or conceit.
rows.anchor: ولا تصعر خدك للناس: أي لا تولهم شق وجهك، كفعل المتكبر

rows.speaker: ابن خويز منداد
rows.claim: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad interprets the warning as not humiliating oneself without need.
rows.anchor: قال ابن خويز منداد: نهى أن يذل نفسه من غير حاجة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya considers whether the phrase could prohibit begging or abject supplication out of poverty.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يريد: ولا سؤالا ولا ضراعة بالفقر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers the anti-arrogance interpretation because the following words discuss haughtiness and conceit.
rows.anchor: قال: والأول، يعني تأويل ابن عباس والجماعة، أظهر لدلالة ذكر الاختيال والعجز بعده

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains the phrase as turning away from someone, such as shunning a brother after an insult.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ولا تصعر، أراد به الإعراض، كهجره بسب أخيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Asim, and Zayd ibn Ali read “tusaʿʿir”; the other seven use a long alif, while al-Jahdari uses “yuṣaʿʿir.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير، وابن عامر، وعاصم، وزيد بن علي: تصعر، بفتح الصاد وشد العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The advice to enjoin good and reject wrong presumes Luqman first practices right conduct; he therefore warns against pride and boastfulness.
rows.anchor: ولما وصى ابنه بالأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكر، إذ صار هو في نفسه ممتثلا للمعروف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the arrogant person boasts of what God gave him instead of thanking God; boasting about lineage also falls under the term.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: وهو الذي يعدد ما أعطى، ولا يشكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Measured walking avoids both slow, self-important steps and the reckless person’s excessive haste.
rows.anchor: بحيث لا يبطىء، كما يفعل المتنامسون والمتعاجبون

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر المنصور
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Mansur remarks of Abu Amr ibn Ubayd: “You all walk slowly, you all hunt for prey, except Amr ibn Ubayd.”
rows.anchor: ونظر أبو جعفر المنصور إلى أبي عمرو بن عبيد فقال: كلكم يمشي رويدا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says people were warned against the Jews’ hurried gait and the Christians’ creeping gait, and told to walk between them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: كانوا ينهون عن خبب اليهود ودبيب النصارى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to place one’s gaze where one’s foot will land.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه: اجعل بصرك موضع قدمك

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh attributes the hamzated reading “wa-aqṣid” to the Hijaz, explaining it as aiming one’s steps properly.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: وأقصد، بهمزة القطع: أي سدد في مشيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lowering the voice means reducing volume and projection; restraint makes speaking easier and helps listeners understand.
rows.anchor: رفعه وجهارته، والغض: رد طموح الشيء، كالصوت والنظر والزمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs once praised powerful voices; a cited poem repeatedly uses “jahīr” to praise a man’s loud and impressive qualities.
rows.anchor: وكانت العرب تفتخر بجهارة الصوت، وتمدح به في الجاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most dissonant” is an unusual comparative formed from a passive verb; it refers to all animal sounds, with the donkey as an extreme insult.
rows.anchor: وأنكر: أفعل، إن بني من فعل المفعول، كقولهم: أشغل من ذات النحيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison omits its marker, turning raised human voices into donkey braying by metaphor for the strongest possible rebuke.
rows.anchor: شبه الرافعون أصواتهم بالحمير، وأصواتهم بالنهاق، ولم يؤت بأداة التشبيه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says idolaters boasted of loud voices, so they are answered that, if loudness were good, donkeys would have been favored with it.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: كان المشركون يتفاخرون برفع الأصوات، فرد عليهم بأنه لو كان خيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent speaker of the donkey comparison is Luqman, warning his son against loudness; another view makes it God’s rebuttal to boastful idolaters.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: إن أنكر الأصوات لصوت الحمير من كلام لقمان لابنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation maps measured walking to restraint in actions and lowered voice to restraint in unnecessary speech.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واقصد في مشيك: إشارة إلى الأفعال، واغضض من صوتك: إشارة إلى الأقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three poetic examples illustrate Arabic counterfactuals introduced by “law,” a construction also used in the verse about trees as pens.
rows.anchor: ولو أنها عصفورة لحسبتها ... مسومة تدعو عبيدا وأيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the majority’s nominative “and the sea,” the waw is most naturally circumstantial and “the sea” is the subject of “would supply it.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الواو في قوله: والبحر، في قراءة من رفع، وهم الجمهور، واو الحال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the sea clause as coordinated with the preceding clause about trees and the conditional “if.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: عطفا على محل إن ومعمولها على ولو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says that coordination only works on al-Mubarrad’s disputed view that “anna” occupies a subject position after “law.”
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يتم إلا على رأي المبرد، حيث زعم أن أن في موضع رفع على الفاعلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians coordinate the sea with “anna,” but that would put a bare subject after “law,” ordinarily allowed only in poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض النحويين: هو عطف على أن، لأنها في موضع رفع بالابتداء

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abd Allah reads “and a sea” as an indefinite nominative; the waw can mark a circumstantial clause or coordinate it with earlier material.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: وبحر يمده، بالتنكير بالرفع، والواو للحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use “yمده” with yāʾ; Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas use feminine tāʾ, while other named readers use the form from “amadda.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يمده بالياء، من مد وابن مسعود، وابن عباس: بتاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad reads “the sea is its ink”; Ibn Atiyya calls “مداده” a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وجعفر بن محمد: والبحر مداده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Seven seas” signals abundance rather than a literal limit; the form “seas” is a paucity plural that matches the number’s form.
rows.anchor: لا يراد به الاقتصار على هذا العدد، بل جيء به للكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted meaning is that if pens and all the sea’s ink wrote God’s words, they would run out before His words did.
rows.anchor: ما نفدت، والمعنى: ولو أن أشجار الأرض أقلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This image parallels the verse saying the sea would be ink for God’s words; the supply would be exhausted while His words remained.
rows.anchor: كما قال: لو كان البحر مدادا لكلمات ربي الآية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari asks how the circumstantial sea clause can lack a pronoun linking it to its subject and proposes “its sea,” referring to earth.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: زعمت أن قوله: والبحر يمده، حال في أحد وجهي الرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says an independent nominal clause introduced by a circumstantial waw needs no linking pronoun; it is unlike a circumstantial adverb.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي جعله سؤالا وجوابا من واضح النحو الذي لا يجهله المبتدءون فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading “the sea” as “its sea” works only under the Kufan view that the definite article can replace a pronoun.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: ويجوز، فلا يجوز إلا على رأي الكوفيين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the singular “a tree” as distributing the image tree by tree until every individual tree becomes a pen.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: لم قيل: من شجرة، على التوحيد دون اسم الجنس الذي هو شجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can use an indefinite singular after “of” to mean an entire plural class, as in verses about any sign, mercy, or creature.
rows.anchor: ونظيره: ما ننسخ من آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each tree has many branches that could each be cut into a pen, producing a quantity beyond reckoning except by God.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الكلام من المبالغة في تكثير الأقلام والمداد ما ينبغي أن يتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may intend to remain in one place until burial, yet be buried somewhere never imagined.
rows.anchor: وربما أقامت بمكان ناوية أن لا تفارقه إلى أن تدفن به، ثم تدفن في مكان لم يخطر لها ببال قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is described with knowledge rather than “knowing by cunning,” because the latter word suggests trickery; God is never called “al-dārī.”
rows.anchor: وأسند العلم إلى الله، والدراية للنفس، لما في الدراية من معنى الختل والحيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan dismisses a pre-Islamic poet’s calling God “al-dārī” as coarse ignorance about which divine attributes are permitted.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: لا هم لا أدري وأنت الداري فقول عربي جلف جاهلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers say “in which land”; Musa al-Aswari and Ibn Abi Abla use the feminine form, a rare agreement with “death.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بأي أرض. وقرأ موسى الأسواري، وابن أبي عبلة: بأية أرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative constructions in “what it earns” and “which land it dies in” are syntactically suspended by “knows”; the latter phrase attaches to “dies.”
rows.anchor: وتدري معلقة في الموضعين. فالجملة من قوله: ماذا تكسب في موضع مفعول تدري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These five matters are named because they answer a question; God alone knows them, though He also knows countless other things.
rows.anchor: ووقع الإخبار بأن الله استأثر بعلمه هذه الخمس، لأنها جواب لسائل سأل

none: Qur’anic verse text only; no commentary point in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Jawf” means the interior or cavity; its plural is “ajwāf.”
rows.anchor: الجوف: معروف، وجمعه أجواف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Yathrib” is the Prophet’s city, or a district within the city.
rows.anchor: يثرب: مدينة الرسول، عليه السلام، وقيل: أرض المدينة في ناحية منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “ḥanjara” is the top of the throat; the “ḥulqūm” is the passage for food and drink.
rows.anchor: الحنجرة: رأس الغلصمة، وهي منتهى الحلقوم والحلقوم: مدخل الطعام والشراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aqṭār” means surrounding regions or sides; its singular is “quṭr,” with “qitr” also reported.
rows.anchor: الأقطار: النواحي، واحدها قطر، ويقال: قتر بالتاء، لغة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “ʿawwaqa” means to hold someone back from a matter or make him hesitate.
rows.anchor: عوق عن كذا: تثبط عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Saliqahu” can mean to strike or address someone boldly; a poet uses it in a line about striking Murad and Sadaʾ.
rows.anchor: سلقه: اجترأ عليه وضربه، ويقال: صلقه بالصاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same root describes eloquent, forceful speech, as in “a salāq or mislāq orator” and “a salāq tongue.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: سلقه: خاطبه مخاطبة بليغة، ومنه خطيب سلاق ومسلاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Suḥub” are vows or undertakings a person does not necessarily bind himself to fulfill; “naḥb” can also mean death.
rows.anchor: السحب: النذر، والشيء الذي لا يلتزمه الإنسان ويعتقد الوفاء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets al-Harith and Jarir use “naḥb” for a great undertaking or commitment; Jarir writes of horses running upon a “naḥb.”
rows.anchor: وقال جرير: بطخفة جالدنا الملوك وخيلنا ... عشية بسطام جرين على نحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ṣayāṣī” means fortresses or defenses; its singular is “ṣayṣiya,” and it can name anything used for protection.
rows.anchor: الصياصي: الحصون، واحدها صيصية، وهي كل ما يمتنع به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word also names horns, rooster spurs, and iron hooks used by weavers; Duraid’s poem evokes hooks striking stretched fabric.
rows.anchor: والصياصي أيضا: شوك الحاكة، ويتخذ من حديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Uswa” means an exemplar or model; the hamza can be pronounced with ḍamma or kasra.
rows.anchor: الأسوة: القدوة، وتضم همزته وتكسر

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth defines “tabarruj” as displaying a woman’s charms of face and body, together with a pleasing look from her eye.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: تبرجت: أبدت محاسنها من وجهها وجسدها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines “tabarruj” as displaying adornments that provoke men’s desire and relates the term to a wide or prominent feature.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: تخرج محاسنها مما تستدعي به شهوة الرجال

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda explains “waṭar” as a need or desire, supported by a line about youth having satisfied a desire.
rows.anchor: الوطر، قال أبو عبيدة: كالأرب، وأنشد للربيع بن أصبغ

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad defines “waṭar” as desire or love and illustrates it with a line about enjoying a beloved’s meeting.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: الوطر: الشهوة والمحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A jilbab is a garment larger than a head-covering.
rows.anchor: الجلباب: ثوب أكبر من الخمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura is Medinan; addressing Muhammad as “Prophet” or “Messenger” honors and elevates him, unlike addressing other prophets by name.
rows.anchor: وتقدم أن نداءه، صلى الله عليه وسلم: يا أيها النبي، يا أيها الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses Muhammad’s name when reporting his messengership, but can use his title when identifying his role without that announcement.
rows.anchor: وحيث ذكره على سبيل الإخبار عنه بأنه رسوله، صرح باسمه فقال: محمد رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fear God tells an already pious Prophet to persist and grow in piety; if he is commanded, others are even more so.
rows.anchor: وأمره بالتقوى للمتلبس بها، أمر بالديمومة عليها والازدياد منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats the words as addressed to the Prophet in form but intended for his community.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو خطاب له لفظا، وهو لأمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One revelation report says the Prophet hoped for Jewish converts, treated hypocritical pledgers gently, and was warned against their deceptive counsel.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه لما قدم المدينة، وكان يحب إسلام اليهود، فبايعه ناس منهم على النفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Abu Sufyan, Ikrima, and Abu al-Aʿwar came during a truce and asked Muhammad to affirm their idols’ intercession; the believers were angered.
rows.anchor: وروي أيضا أن أبا سفيان، وعكرمة بن أبي جهل، وأبا الأعور السلمي قدموا في الموادعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports together explain the warning against obeying Meccan unbelievers and Medinan hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وناسب أن نهاه عن طاعة الكفار، وهم المتظاهرون به، وعن طاعة المنافقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third revelation report says Meccans offered half their wealth and a marriage alliance if Muhammad returned to their religion; Medinan hypocrites threatened to kill him.
rows.anchor: وروي أن أهل مكة دعوه إلى أن يرجع إلى دينهم، ويعطوه شطر أموالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura’s opening matches the previous sura’s ending: after unbelievers demand judgment, Muhammad is told to fear God and reject their requests.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة أول هذه السورة لآخر ما قبلها واضحة، وهو أنه حكى أنهم يستعجلون الفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Knowing, Wise” means God knows right from wrong and benefit from harm, and places matters according to wisdom.
rows.anchor: عليما بالصواب من الخطأ، والمصلحة من المفسدة حكيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the names console the Messenger: God knows who is pious and wisely guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي تسلية للرسول، أي عليما بمن يتقي، حكيما في هدي من شاء وإضلال من شاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following revelation means following the Qur’an alone and leaving the practices of pre-Islamic custom.
rows.anchor: ثم أمره باتباع ما أوحي إليه، وهو القرآن، والاقتصار عليه، وترك مراسيم الجاهلية

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr reads both occurrences of “you do” with a yāʾ; the other seven readers use a tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو: بما يعملون، الأولى والثانية بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the first occurrence, the yāʾ reading can be a shift of address or match the preceding command to follow revelation.
rows.anchor: فجاز في الأولى أن يكون من باب الالتفات، وجاز أن يكون مناسبا لقوله: واتبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After commanding reliance on revelation, God commands the Prophet to entrust his affairs to Him; the phrase “God is sufficient” was explained earlier.
rows.anchor: ثم أمره بتفويض أمره إلى الله. وتقدم الكلام في كفى بالله في أول ما وقع في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report identifies a man from Banu Fihr as Abu Maʿmar Jamil ibn Maʿmar; another gives the name Humaid ibn Maʿmar.
rows.anchor: روي أنه كان في بني فهر رجل فيهم يقال له: أبو معمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant report gives his name as Humaid ibn Maʿmar ibn Habib ibn Wahb ibn Haritha ibn Jumah.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حميد بن معمر بن حبيب بن وهب بن حارثة بن جمح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He claimed to have two hearts, called himself “the two-hearted,” and boasted he understood better than Muhammad; news of Badr left him deranged.
rows.anchor: يدعي أن له قلبين، ويقال له: ذو القلبين، وكان يقول: أنا أذكى من محمد وأفهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the verse concerns people who claim that one inner self commands them and another restrains them.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هم جماعة، يقول الواحد منهم: نفس تأمرني ونفس تنهاني

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says a hypocrite claimed Muhammad had two hearts because he could move between tasks and return to the first.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن بعض المنافقين قال إن محمدا له قلبان، لأنه ربما كان في شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One heart cannot be duplicated usefully: identical hearts would be redundant, while different hearts could produce contradictory mental states at once.
rows.anchor: ولم يجعل الله للإنسان قلبين، لأنه إما أن يفعل أحدهما مثل ما يفعل الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the body cavity makes the image vivid, as in the Qur’anic expression about hearts inside chests.
rows.anchor: للتصوير والتجلي للمدلول عليه، كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary in the form of “the wives whom you declare as your mothers,” including hamza and yāʾ pronunciations.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قالون وقنبل: اللائي هنا، وفي المجادلة والطلاق

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads the ẓihār verb with a doubled hāʾ after a light ẓāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: تظهرون، بضم التاء وتخفيف الظاء وشد الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since ẓihār functioned as divorce in pre-Islamic usage, its verb describes distancing oneself from a wife, as from a divorced woman.
rows.anchor: وعدي الفعل بمن، لأن الظهار كان طلاقا في الجاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metaphor of the back intensified the prohibition; people claimed intercourse with a woman facing upward would make the child cross-eyed.
rows.anchor: ولكونهم كانوا يقولون: يحرم إتيان المرأة وظهرها للسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same image appears in 22:46, where the Qur’an speaks of hearts within chests.
rows.anchor: كما قال تعالى: ولكن تعمى القلوب التي في الصدور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage denies that a wife made unlawful by ẓihār becomes a mother: a mother is served and honored, while a wife is subject to marital use.
rows.anchor: وما جعل أزواجكم: لم يجعل تعالى الزوجة المظاهر منها أما، لأن الأم مخدومة مخفوض لها جناح الذل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary in the spelling and pronunciation of “the wives whom you declare as your mothers,” including hamza and yāʾ forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قالون وقنبل: اللائي هنا، وفي المجادلة والطلاق: بالهمز من غير ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nine readings are listed for forms of “you perform ẓihār”; they all refer to saying to a wife, “You are to me like my mother’s back.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم: تظاهرون بالتاء للخطاب، وفي المجادلة: بالياء للغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb derives from the utterance “you are as my mother’s back,” like verbs formed from the spoken expressions “labbayk” and “uff.”
rows.anchor: والمعنى: قال لها: أنت علي كظهر أمي. فتلك الأفعال مأخوذة من هذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Haritha was captured young, bought by Hakim ibn Hizam for Khadija, given to the Prophet, freed, and called Zayd ibn Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وروي أن زيد بن حارثة من كلب سبي صغيرا، فاشتراه حكيم بن حزام لعمته خديجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In pre-Islamic times and early Islam, adoption could make another man’s son an heir.
rows.anchor: وكانوا في الجاهلية وصدر الإسلام إذا تبنى الرجل ولد غيره صار يرثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Adʿiyāʾ” is an anomalous plural of “daʿiyy”; its expected plural would be “daʿāyā,” though similar irregular plurals occur.
rows.anchor: وأدعياء: جمع دعي، فعيل بمعنى مفعول، جاء شاذا، وقياسه فعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Natural sonship reflects actual lineage, whereas adoption adds a nominal attribution; one person cannot be both original and non-original son.
rows.anchor: والبنوة تقتضي التأصل في النسب، والدعوة إلصاق عارض بالتسمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling adopted sons biological sons is only a verbal claim without matching belief; God’s statement matches outward and inward reality.
rows.anchor: ذلكم: أي دعاؤهم أبناء مجرد قول لا حقيقة لمدلوله، إذ لا يواطئ اللفظ الاعتقاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God guides the path” refers either to truth, namely naming adopted children after their fathers, or to the path of religion and faith.
rows.anchor: وهو يهدي السبيل: أي سبيل الحق، وهو قوله: ادعوهم لآبائهم، أو سبيل الشرع والإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use “yahdi”; Qatada reads it with a ḍamma and doubled dāl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يهدي مضارع هدى وقتادة: بضم الياء وفتح الهاء وشد الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “More just” means fairer; those who know the biological father should use that lineage, as with Zayd and Salim.
rows.anchor: وأقسط: أفعل التفضيل، وتقدم الكلام فيه في أواخر البقرة، ومعناه: أعدل

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says Abu Bakra recited the verse and called himself a brother and client because he did not know his father.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري أن أبا بكرة قرأ هذه الآية ثم قال: أنا ممن لا يعرف أبوه

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi says one should claim even a lowly father rather than invent lineage; hadith transmitters identify Abu Bakra as Nafiʿ ibn al-Harith.
rows.anchor: قال الرازي: ولو علم والله أباه حمارا لانتمى إليه، ورجال الحديث يقولون فيه: نفيع بن الحارث

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report warns that anyone who knowingly claims another father will be forbidden Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «من ادعى إلى غير أبيه متعمدا حرم الله عليه الجنة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view excuses mistaken attribution before the prohibition, but Abu Hayyan rejects it because conduct before the rule cannot be called an error.
rows.anchor: فيما أخطأتم به، قيل: رفع الحرج عنهم فيما كان قبل النهي، وهذا ضعيف لا يوصف بالخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view excuses a slip of the tongue, accidental or affectionate, such as calling a child “son” or an elder “father.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: فيما سبق إليه اللسان. إما على سبيل الغلط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only deliberate attribution incurs blame; God forgives deliberate offenders who repent and lifts blame for mistakes.
rows.anchor: وكان الله غفورا للعامد إذا تاب، رحيما حيث رفع الجناح عن المخطئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is more compassionate toward believers and directs them to salvation, whereas their own selves can lead them toward destruction.
rows.anchor: كونه، عليه السلام، أولى بالمؤمنين من أنفسهم: أي أرأف بهم وأعطف عليهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says he pulls believers back from Hell while they throw themselves into it like moths.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله، عليه السلام: «أنا آخذ بحجزكم عن النار وأنتم تقتحمون فيها تقحم الفراش»

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says every prophet is the father of his community in religion.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: كل نبي أبو أمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading in the codices of Ubay and Abd Allah adds “and he is their father,” meaning in religion.
rows.anchor: وكذلك في مصحف أبي، وقراءة عبد الله: وأزواجه أمهاتهم: وهو أب لهم، يعني في الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s “these are my daughters” may mean believing women as his daughters in religion; believers are likewise called brothers in 49:10.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل في قول لوط عليه السلام: هؤلاء بناتي، إنه أراد المؤمنات، أي بناته في الدين

rows.speaker: عنه عليه السلام
rows.claim: The Prophet says he is closer to every believer in this life and the next: property goes to heirs, but debt and dependents come to him.
rows.anchor: وعنه عليه السلام: «ما من مؤمن إلا وأنا أولى به في الدنيا والآخرة. واقرأوا إن شئتم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An unrestricted reading makes the Prophet foremost in every matter, more beloved than oneself and with a ruling that outranks one’s own.
rows.anchor: قيل: وأطلق في قوله تعالى: أولى بالمؤمنين: أي في كل شيء، ولم يقيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that this unrestricted meaning would require wording that makes believers the subject and the Prophet the object of priority.
rows.anchor: ولو أريد هذا المعنى، لكان التركيب: المؤمنون أولى بالنبي منهم بأنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s wives are like mothers in respect and honor and in some rulings, including the prohibition on marrying them.
rows.anchor: وأزواجه أمهاتهم: أي مثل أمهاتهم في التوقير والاحترام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view applies the status to every woman ever named the Prophet’s wife; others exclude divorced wives or limit it to wives he consummated marriage with.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: وأزواجه: كل من أطلق عليها أنها زوجة له، عليه السلام، من طلقها ومن لم يطلقها

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar began to stone a woman divorced by the Prophet who remarried; when she said she had not been veiled or called a mother, he stopped.
rows.anchor: وهم عمر برجم امرأة فارقها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، ونكحت بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse replaces inheritance through religious brotherhood or migration with priority for blood relatives.
rows.anchor: كان أولا بالمدينة، توارث بأخوة الإسلام وبالهجرة، ثم حكم تعالى بأن أولي الأرحام أحق بالتوارث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In God’s book” may mean the Preserved Tablet or the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: في كتاب الله، أي في اللوح المحفوظ، أو في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Believers and emigrants” most naturally means relatives take priority over those who inherited by faith or migration.
rows.anchor: من المؤمنين والمهاجرين، أي أولى من المؤمنين الذين كانوا يتوارثون بمجرد الإيمان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows “from among the believers and emigrants” to specify which relatives have priority over unrelated people.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يجوز أن يكون بيانا لأولي الأرحام، أي الأقرباء من هؤلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In the book” can refer either to the Preserved Tablet or to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: في الكتاب: إما اللوح، وإما القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Written down” means firmly established in lines and serves as a closing statement for the preceding rules.
rows.anchor: مسطورا: أي مثبتا بالأسطار، وهذه الجملة مستأنفة كالخاتمة

rows.speaker: الحوفي وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Hawfi and Ibn Atiyya allow the temporal “when” to be governed by “written down,” as if the pact were recorded in the Mother of the Book.
rows.anchor: والعامل في إذ، قاله الحوفي وابن عطية، يجوز أن يكون مسطورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “when” is governed by an implied “remember”; the covenant charges prophets to deliver God’s messages without fear or hope of gain.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العامل: واذكر حين أخذنا، وهذا الميثاق هو في تبليغ رسالات الله

rows.speaker: قتادة والحسن وعطاء وابن الحنفية
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Ibn al-Hanafiyya take “your allies” broadly: relatives or unrelated people, believers or unbelievers, may receive kindness and a bequest.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عموم قوله: إلى أوليائكم، فيشمل جميع أقسامه، من قريب وأجنبي

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن زيد والرماني
rows.claim: Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and al-Rummani restrict the allies in this exception to believers; the context supports their view.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وابن زيد، والرماني وغيره: إلى أوليائكم، مخصوص بالمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blood kinship does not disappear for an unbeliever; what is excluded is affection and allegiance as though the person were an Islamic client.
rows.anchor: لكن ولاية النسب لا تدفع في الكافر، إنما تدفع في أن تلقي إليه بالمودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception implies kindness to allies in benefits other than inheritance, since the text elides that prior category.
rows.anchor: وهذا الاستثناء في قوله: إلا أن تفعلوا هو مما يفهم من الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To your allies” uses “to” because the implied phrase is to convey benefits to them; “written down” means firmly recorded.
rows.anchor: وعدى بإلى، لأن المعنى: إلا أن توصلوا إلى أوليائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The covenant passage concludes the preceding rules, some inherited from pre-Islamic practice and others abrogated in Islam.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة مستأنفة كالخاتمة، لما ذكر من الأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s covenant with the prophets concerns conveying laws and calling people to Him, so Muhammad is not novel in his mission.
rows.anchor: وإذ أخذنا من النبيين ميثاقهم: أي في تبليغ الشرائع والدعاء إلى الله

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says God took their covenant to convey the message.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: أخذ ميثاقهم بالتبليغ

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the prophets covenanted to affirm one another, announce Muhammad is God’s Messenger, and announce no prophet follows him.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: بتصديق بعضهم بعضا، والإعلان بأن محمدا رسول الله

rows.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj and others place the covenant at humanity’s extraction from Adam as atoms, including all duties of prophecy.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج وغيره: الذي أخذ عليهم وقت استخراج البشر من صلب آدم كالذر

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A similar account of the primordial covenant is transmitted from Ubay ibn Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: وروي نحوه عن أبي بن كعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Five prophets are named after the general category either because they are people of resolve or because of their rank; Muhammad is first for superiority and followers.
rows.anchor: وخص هؤلاء الخمسة بالذكر بعد دخولهم في جملة النبيين. وقيل: هم أولو العزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah precedes Muhammad in 42:13 because that verse presents Islam as the ancient religion first entrusted to Noah and renewed through later prophets.
rows.anchor: وقدم نوح في آية الشورى في قوله: شرع لكم من الدين ما وصى به نوحا الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second mention of the covenant repeats the first to emphasize its attribute; describing it as “thick” metaphorically magnifies its sanctity and burden.
rows.anchor: والميثاق الثاني هو الأول، وكرر لأجل صفته. والغلظ: من صفة الأجسام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the “weighty covenant” an oath sworn by God to fulfill the charge.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الميثاق الغليظ: اليمين بالله على الوفاء بما حمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “so He may ask” could mark an eventual result, though its apparent function is purpose.
rows.anchor: واللام في ليسئل، قيل: يحتمل أن تكون لام الصيرورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan takes the lām as purposive: God commissioned prophets so He could question people and establish proof, reward the truthful, and punish unbelievers.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنها لام كي، أي بعثنا الرسل وأخذنا عليهم المواثيق في التبليغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their truthfulness” may mean fidelity to the covenant, with “their covenant” elided, or affirmation of the prophets, with its object elided.
rows.anchor: والهاء في صدقهم عائدة عليهم، ومفعول صدقهم محذوف تقديره: عن صدقهم عهده

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa says the prophets will be asked about what their communities answered them.
rows.anchor: أو ليسأل الأنبياء الذي أجابتهم به أممهم، حكاه علي بن عيسى

rows.speaker: ابن شجرة
rows.claim: Ibn Shajara says the question concerns whether the prophets fulfilled the covenant taken from them.
rows.anchor: أو ليسأل عن الوفاء بالميثاق الذي أخذه عليهم، حكاه ابن شجرة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the prophets will be questioned about delivering the message to their people; if prophets are questioned, others are even more liable.
rows.anchor: أو ليسأل الأنبياء عن تبليغهم الرسالة إلى قومهم، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also says “the truthful” means those who conveyed the message on behalf of the messengers.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أيضا: ليسئل الصادقين، أراد المؤدين عن الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls God’s favor at the Battle of the Trench and the related events involving Banu Qurayza.
rows.anchor: ذكرهم الله تعالى بنعمته عليهم في غزوة الخندق، وما اتصل بها من أمر بني قريظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal “when” is governed by “favor,” specifying the time the armies arrived.
rows.anchor: وإذ معمولة لنعمة، أي إنعامه عليكم وقت مجيء الجنود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confederate forces numbered ten thousand; Quraysh and their allies made up four thousand under Abu Sufyan.
rows.anchor: والجنود كانوا عشرة آلاف، قريش ومن تابعهم من الأحابيش في أربعة آلاف يقودهم أبو سفيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account names the leaders of Banu Asad, Ghatafan, Banu Amir, and Sulaym among the allied forces.
rows.anchor: وبنو أسد يقودهم طليحة، وغطفان يقودهم عيينة، وبنو عامر يقودهم عامر بن الطفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jewish Nadir were led by Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq; Qurayza’s chief was Kaʿb ibn Asad, who broke his treaty with Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وبنو قريظة سيدهم كعب بن أسد، وكان بينه وبين الرسول عهد
